verdict: Caution: lend selectively to job-work machining units with verified order books and clean receivables; avoid capex-heavy fabrication units exposed to delayed industrial payments.
title: Ghaziabad fabrication & machining workshops: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Ghaziabad fabrication or machining workshop buys steel, castings and consumables, cuts and turns them on lathes, CNC and press machines, and sells the output as job-work or components to nearby OEMs and traders.** Cash comes in per job or per purchase order, so the unit's real engine is machine hours and order flow, not balance-sheet size. Ghaziabad is described locally as a manufacturing hub built on engineering skill across metal work and textiles [2][3]. **Value sits in the machine and the skilled operator; cash sits in receivables from the industrial buyer.** So when a proposal lands, check the customer list and the ageing first, not the plant. ## Where the cash cycle bites
**Cost is dominated by steel and consumables, power, wages and machine depreciation; pricing power is thin because job-work rates are quoted per piece against many small competitors.** Working capital is the whole game: inventory of raw steel plus receivables from OEM buyers. The ICRA fabric methodology notes working capital is driven by inventory holding and receivables [8], and the same logic holds for metal job-work. **Capex is lumpy — one CNC or press can absorb a year's profit — so term debt tenure matters more than rate.** Rating guidance flags that longer-tenure debt covers similar leverage more comfortably [9]. So when a proposal lands, check whether term loan tenure matches the machine's earning life; if the ask is a short-tenure loan for a long-life machine, ask for the repayment source. ## What has changed now
**The official data pack reads Caution at 57 for this cluster, and the local news is negative: Ghaziabad industrialists are protesting what they call government neglect and restrictive policies [1].** That is a facilities-and-policy grievance, not a demand collapse, but it tells you approvals and utilities may be slow. Uttar Pradesh GST collections are running +14.2% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D], a genuine local tailwind. **Against that, bank credit is growing +24.4% YoY versus activity at +6.1% [D] — money is chasing this space faster than output, so underwriting discipline is what protects us.** Peer results are strong but are large listed forgers, not Ghaziabad workshops: Ramkrishna Forgings revenue +54.9% with EBITDA margin 18.2% [7], Balu Forge EBITDA margin 27.2% [6], Kranti Industries revenue +20.3% YoY [5]. Treat these as direction, not benchmarks for a 20-machine shed. **Avoid pure fabrication units bidding on single large orders with one buyer, and any unit whose growth is funded entirely by us while its own receivables stretch.** Local sources say little specific about Ghaziabad workshop finances, so lean on first principles and the peer direction above. ## Structure and monthly discipline
**Structure as cash-credit against stock and receivables with a drawing power recalculated monthly, plus a term loan only where the machine has a named buyer contract.** Take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, GST returns, and electricity bills — power demand in UP is +8.6% Apr-to-date [D], so a unit's own consumption trend is a clean activity check. **Covenant on debtor days and on customer concentration; if top buyer exceeds half of sales, ask for a diversion-of-sales undertaking.**
watch: Filing gap or falling turnover vs last year -> freeze fresh drawing power and visit site
Two consecutive months of falling units -> ask for order book and check machine idle time
Debtor days stretch beyond agreed covenant -> reduce limit and seek buyer confirmation
Single buyer crosses half of sales -> ask for diversification plan before renewal
Stock value diverges from physical count -> revalue drawing power and inspect
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
